PM · ABC listen

US patience wears as China withholds plane

Broadcast Tuesday, 3 April 2001 · Reporter: Tom O'Byrne

← Full PM episode — Tuesday, 3 April 2001

MARK COLVIN: There's no lessening of tension tonight between the United States and China despite Beijing's assurances that US officials will get access tonight to the crew of the grounded American spy plane.

On the American side, there's barely concealed fury that it's taken 60 hours just to get a promise of consular access to their own personnel. On the Chinese side the newsagency AFP quotes an official on Hainan Island as saying "the Americans want everything, they want us to repair the plane and let the crew go, they make it sound as simple as having a meal, but things are not that simple".

Almost certainly what both sides are really thinking about is not so much the people, as the technology.

Chinese officials say the crew has disembarked and been taken to a nearby military base, but they've refused to say whether the spy plane has been boarded by Chinese military personnel.

And the Americans are extremely worried about what the Chinese may be able to extract from a close inspection of the plane.

Tonight the Chinese Foreign Ministry has been briefing journalists in Beijing, and the indications are that if anything, they're cranking up the hostilities.

Our correspondent Tom O'Byrne has been at the briefing.

TOM O'BYRNE: Mark, picking up on your comments that there should be concern among the American side in this incident, the, there is every indication that the Chinese authorities on Hainan Island have actually inspected this plane.

And there is an indication from the Foreign Ministry official, Dubung Zhou, that there is a long, a long way before this incident is over.

MARK COLVIN: What indication do you mean, what, what are they saying exactly?

TOM O'BYRNE: Well we're hearing from Dubung Zhou that the Chinese have not, despite the American concerns, violated any agreements about what this plane actually represents. You'll remember that the US side have considered this plane and its content and its crew to be American territory. The Chinese, in quite strong language for diplomats, have said that this is nothing like the case. That this plane has violated Chinese air space, it has violated Chinese sovereignty by landing without permission on Chinese soil, and so therefore in this regard, the Chinese say they have every right to investigate this.

They say that the crew are safe and they have allowed this meeting with the US consular officials, but as far as the plane is concerned, it seems to be a different story. The quote specifically from Dubung Zhou was "how come American territory can move to the Chinese mainland. Now that is a very strong indication in diplomatic terms that the Chinese - if they've not boarded the plane already and started to inspect it - that that is one of their plans, one of their aims.

MARK COLVIN: Well.

TOM O'BYRNE: A serious development no doubt.

MARK COLVIN: Well I mean, clearly Embassy grounds for instance, are diplomatic territory, and the Chinese have all, have usually respected that, but they, what they're saying is that they simply don't accept this claim that the aeroplane in some way gets diplomatic status as it were?

TOM O'BYRNE: Precisely. The point that was made by the Foreign Ministry officials here was that this aeroplane is not an ordinary aircraft, but a military reconis, a military reconnaissance plane. They were saying that after damaging the Chinese aircraft - and remember the Chinese have never admitted any fault in this incident - after damaging the Chinese jet craft, in or near Chinese airspace, without permission they landed on Chinese soil.

So they're saying following that, that China has every right to investigate this event.

MARK COLVIN: But you were, you were telling us last night, weren't you, that the Taiwanese intercept of, of the traffic between the two planes, suggested that the Chinese fighter had actually threatened the American plane with - presumably a missile attack or an attack of some sort - and that the Americans had radioed Mayday, and so essentially the Americans would be saying that they were forced down?

TOM O'BYRNE: Precisely. Now we haven't heard any independent confirmation of those Taiwanese claims, but they were coming from American trained military intelligence analysts on Taiwan Island. Those, that claim hasn't been confirmed or denied by the Americans - that's now been in circulation nearly 24 hours - and the, the development today suggests that the Chinese will take this very, very different, this very very different tack from the line that the Americans have been pushing - that this plane and its crew are protected in effect, the same way as embassies are protected.

They say that this plane violated their airspace and even more so, according to the Chinese, they're saying that they want - because China needs to, ... because the United States needs to bear responsibility in this, they've made protests to the United States Ambassador here in, in Beijing, Admiral Joe Prear, that the Chinese wants the United States to stop all military reconnaissance flights anywhere near Chinese territory, until this is sorted out.

So they're, they're taking a very, very serious hard line on this issue.

MARK COLVIN: Now I was reading that the, the normal American military standing order in this case would have been that the crew should resist any attempt to, by a foreign force to get into the plane. Do we know anything about what transpired, whether there was resistance?

TOM O'BYRNE: I think the information on that score will start to emerge once the consular officials and the attaches from the embassy here in Beijing and from the Consulate in Guangzhou will have had a chance to talk to the, the pilot and the crew.

MARK COLVIN: And do we know when that's going to be now?

TOM O'BYRNE: Well we know that it's taking place tonight local time, tonight in Chinese time. We don't know whether that's face to face or over the phone. But what we're being told as far as the Chinese are concerned, that the, the crew are safe and well, but the plane is a different matter altogether.

MARK COLVIN: Now all of this indicates on the, on the, in the broader spectrum if you like, that the Chinese . I mean it's not just an issue about a plane is it, because it's, it's been elevated by the fact that George W Bush has said that, has put China in this new category of strategic rival, rather than partner. This is all, all about a complete realignment of Chinese American relations really, and it, it looks as if both sides are going to take a very hard line.

TOM O'BYRNE: Definitely, and that point was underscored by comments from Dubung Zhou who was saying that earlier today, when meeting senior Saudi Arabian Government officials, no less than Jiang Zemin the President of China, also weighed in with his views on this issue. He too was taking the line that it was the American Government fault from the start this issue.

They are particularly concerned that there is international worry about 24 crewman and the plane on Chinese territory, but no concern for the missing pilot - the missing Chinese pilot from the jet fighter that collided with this American plane. That search is still underway, we're seeing on Chinese television pictures of some 20 ships and dozens of planes that are searching the South China Sea, still without success.

But the point that Jiang Zemin was making, that gives an indication that this is really reached, this has really reached a new level of tension, that he is saying "I care very deeply about this pilot, and nothing will be done until this pilot is recovered".

Now that is giving an indication - at least on this early stage, this early interpretation - that there'll be no movement on the plane or indeed on possibly the return of these crewman to the United States, until there is some closure on what has happened to this pilot.

MARK COLVIN: Tom O'Byrne, and it's been confirmed that the Chinese have now promised the Americans that they will be able to, at least, see their crew tonight.
